scenes.tts: The lining of your small intestine is a single layer of cells. Yet it moves glucose one way, from the gut into the blood. At the same time, it keeps the gut's contents from seeping in between the cells. How can one thin sheet do both? It can only if each cell knows which way is up, and the gaps between cells are sealed.
scenes.visual: Three cells form a sheet with gut above and blood below; a glucose arrow runs gut to blood, gut contents try to enter a gap and are crossed out, a question mark sits on the cell.
scenes.narration: The lining of your small intestine is a single layer of cells. Yet it moves glucose one way, from the gut into the blood. At the same time, it keeps the gut's contents from seeping in between the cells. How can one thin sheet do both? It can only if each cell knows which way is up, and the gaps between cells are sealed.

scenes.tts: Each cell in the sheet has two faces. The apical face looks into the gut. The basolateral face looks at the neighbouring cells, and below them, a thin mat called the basement membrane. The two faces carry different proteins and lipids. That difference is called apicobasal polarity.

scenes.visual: The top membrane of the middle cell lights up and is tagged apical; the sides and base light up and are tagged basolateral; different small shapes sit on each face; a double arrow joins the two faces.
scenes.narration: Each cell in the sheet has two faces. The apical face looks into the gut. The basolateral face looks at the neighbouring cells, and below them, a thin mat called the basement membrane. The two faces carry different proteins and lipids. That difference is called apicobasal polarity.

scenes.tts: In vertebrate epithelia, junctions are stacked in a fixed order. That order is not universal. The tight junction is the most apical. It seals the space between cells. In rat kidney tubules filled with hemoglobin, the tracer stopped at this junction. That placed a barrier there for a protein-sized tracer. It did not show that the junction is closed to ions.

scenes.visual: Zoom on the gap between two cells: a red tight junction bar sits at the top of the stack; hemoglobin tracer dots drift down the gap and pile on the bar; an ions question mark sits below the bar.

scenes.tts: Glucose takes the route through the cell. On the apical face, a sodium glucose symporter called S G L T one carries glucose into the cell with sodium. For human S G L T one in frog oocytes, two sodium ions come in with each sugar. The sodium runs down its gradient into the cell. It drags glucose in against its own.
scenes.caption: Glucose takes the route through the cell. On the apical face, a sodium-glucose symporter called SGLT1 carries glucose into the cell with sodium. For human SGLT1 in frog oocytes, two sodium ions come in with each sugar. The sodium runs down its gradient into the cell. It drags glucose in against its own.
scenes.visual: In the middle cell, SGLT1 on the apical membrane takes in one glucose and two sodium ions together, twice; arrows mark sodium down its gradient and glucose against its own.
scenes.narration: Glucose takes the route through the cell. On the apical face, a sodium-glucose symporter called SGLT1 carries glucose into the cell with sodium. scenes.tts: At the basolateral face, a sodium-independent carrier lets glucose leave. Glucose moves down its concentration gradient by facilitated diffusion. In the standard account, this carrier is GLUT 2. The sodium-potassium pump on the same face uses ATP to push sodium out. It keeps cytosolic sodium low. Without it, the gradient that drives S G L T one runs down.

scenes.visual: GLUT2 appears on the basal membrane and the cell's glucose leaves through it; the sodium-potassium pump appears with an ATP chip and sends the sodium out; the sodium gradient arrow at SGLT1 stays full.
scenes.narration: At the basolateral face, a sodium-independent carrier lets glucose leave. Glucose moves down its concentration gradient by facilitated diffusion. In the standard account, this carrier is GLUT2. The sodium-potassium pump on the same face uses ATP to push sodium out. It keeps cytosolic sodium low. scenes.tts: The polarity matters. Put S G L T one on both faces, and the basolateral copies would pull glucose back in from the blood. That works against absorption. So each face carries its own transporters, and the tight junction seals the gaps. Together they move glucose one way and keep the gut's contents out.

scenes.visual: SGLT1 is placed on the base and glucose flows up from the blood, marked wrong; the base copy turns back into GLUT2, glucose flows gut to blood, and red seals close the gaps against the gut contents.
